Title: Tables for bounds on covering codes
URL: https://old.sztaki.hu/~keri/codes/index.htm
Published: N/A
Author: Gerzson
Highlights:
Tables for bounds on covering codes Tables for Bounds on Covering Codes (The best known lower and upper bounds on the smallest size of a covering code, 2 <= q <= 21) Please report further updates or corrections or classification results to keri@sztaki.hu.

1. Bounds for binary covering codes, listed for n <= 33, R <= 10 [PostScript] [PDF]
2. Bounds for ternary covering codes, listed for n <= 14, R <= 8 [PostScript] [PDF]
3. Bounds for quaternary and quinary covering codes, listed for n <= 11, R <= 8 [PostScript] [PDF]
4. Bounds for q-ary covering codes where (6 <= q <= 10, n <= 10) or (11 <= q <= 21, n <= 8) [PostScript] [PDF]
5. Bounds for mixed ternary/binary covering codes, listed for t+b <= 13, R <= 3 [PostScript] [PDF]

Title: New upper and lower bounds on covering codes 𝐾_𝑞⁢(𝑛,𝑅)for alphabets of size 5≤𝑞≤21
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19872v3
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Let $Kq​(n,R)K_{q}(n,R)$ denote the minimum cardinality of a $qq$-ary code of length $nn$ with covering radius $RR$. We improve the known bounds on $Kq​(n,R)K_{q}(n,R)$ in $8484$ cases ($8383$ distinct cells). Twenty-six upper bounds for $5≤q≤155\leq q\leq 15$ are established by explicit codes, found by local search and by a large neighbourhood search whose evaluations are exact coverage counts over the whole space $ℤqn\mathbb{Z}_{q}^{n}$, computed by a coordinate-wise transform; two examples are $K7​(9,5)≤240K_{7}(9,5)\leq 240$ (previously $323323$) and $K8​(10,5)≤1883K_{8}(10,5)\leq 1883$ (previously $24612461$). Fifty-eight lower bounds for $6≤q≤216\leq q\leq 21$ are obtained from the semidefinite programming bound of Gijswijt and Polak, whose published computations cover $q≤5q\leq 5$, by solving the symmetry-reduced program in multiprecision arithmetic and rounding each dual solution to an exact rational certificate; every certificate is checked by a standalone program in exact arithmetic. The cell $K6​(10,4)K_{6}(10,4)$ is improved from both sides, from $417417$–$29522952$ to $441441$–$27512751$. The codes, the certificates, and the checkers are provided as ancillary files.
...
Upper bounds on $Kq​(n,R)K_{q}(n,R)$ are established by explicit codes and lower bounds by counting or convex-relaxation arguments. The known bounds for $q≥3q\geq 3$ are collected in the tables of Kéri [8], which extend those of [3] and were last revised in November 2011; the tables attribute $9696$ of their upper bounds for $q≥6q\geq 6$ to [7]. Recent lower-bound work concerns small alphabets: Wu and Chen [17] improved binary lower bounds, and Gijswijt and Polak [5] obtained new lower bounds for $q≤5q\leq 5$ from a semidefinite programming hierarchy. Florath [4] formalizes covering-code bounds in a proof assistant. For $q≥6q\geq 6$ we know of no published improvement on either side since 2011, and of none on the upper-bound side for $q≥5q\geq 5$; a search of arXiv, DBLP, OpenAlex, Lobstein’s covering-radius bibliography [11], and the publication lists of the authors active in the area, carried out in August 2026, found none.

Unions of cosets of a linear code. When $qq$ is a prime power and $M=c​qkM=c\,q^{k}$, we search codes of the form $C=⋃i=1c(xi+L)C=\bigcup_{i=1}^{c}(x_{i}+L)$ with $LL$ a linear $[n,k]q[n,k]_{q}$ code. Such a $CC$ has covering radius at most $RR$ if and only if the syndromes of $x1,…,xcx_{1},\dots,x_{c}$ cover the $qn−kq^{n-k}$ syndromes under the coset-leader weights of $LL$, a problem on $qn−kq^{n-k}$ rather than $qnq^{n}$ elements. This search reproduces the tabulated $K8​(8,4)≤512=83K_{8}(8,4)\leq 512=8^{3}$ and $K5​(11,5)≤625=54K_{5}(11,5)\leq 625=5^{4}$ in under a second, whereas the unrestricted search did not reach these sizes; the searches leading to $505505$ and $602602$ start from these codes.

Gijswijt and Polak [5, Theorem 4.18] bound $Kq​(n,R)3K_{q}(n,R)^{3}$ from below by the optimum of a semidefinite program in variables indexed by the orbits of triples of words under $Aut⁡(H⁡(n,q))=Sq≀Sn\mathrm{Aut}(H(n,q))=S_{q}\wr S_{n}$, with positive semidefiniteness constraints from the block diagonalization of the Terwilliger algebra of the Hamming scheme, linear constraints expressing sphere-covering inequalities, and the matrix-cut constraints of their Proposition 4.17. The program is stated in Appendix B. For $q≥3q\geq 3$ its size depends only on $nn$ (at $n=11n=11$: $339339$ variables and $126126$ blocks of order at most $1313$), and $qq$ enters only through the coefficients; the computations published in [5] cover $q≤5q\leq 5$.

Title: Constructions, families, and tables of binary linear covering codes

Author: Alexander A. Davydov, A.Yu. Drozhzhina-Labvinskaya
Highlights:
# Constructions, families, and tables of binary linear covering codes
...
Presents constructions and infinite families of binary linear covering codes with covering radii R=2,3,4. Using these codes, the authors obtain a table of constructive upper bounds on the length function l(r,R) for r/spl les/64 and R=2,3,4, where l(r, R) is the smallest length of a binary linear code with given codimension r and covering radius R. They obtain also upper bounds on l(r, R) for r=21, 28, R=5. Parameters of the constructed codes are better than parameters of previously known codes.>

6. Lower bounds 6.1. The semidefinite program. Gijswijt and Polak [5, Theorem 4.18] bound Kq(n, R) 3 from below by the optimum of a semidefinite program in variables indexed by the orbits of triples of words under Aut(H(n, q)) = Sq ≀ Sn, with positive semidefiniteness constraints from the block diagonalization of the Terwilliger algebra of the Hamming scheme, linear con straints expressing sphere-covering inequalities, and the matrix-cut constraints of their Propo sition 4.17. The program is stated in Appendix B. For q ≥ 3 its size depends only on n (at n = 11: 339 variables and 126 blocks of order at most 13), and q enters only through the coefficients; the computations published in [5] cover q ≤ 5. We reimplemented the reduced program with the generation of all coefficients in exact integer arithmetic. The implementation was checked as follows: (a) for each length 2 ≤ n ≤ 10 an explicit verified code of covering radius R (for 6 ≤ n ≤ 10, codes from Table 1) was substituted into the program and every constraint was checked in exact rational arithmetic, with objective value exactly | C| 3; (b) every coefficient generated for six cells with 3 ≤ q ≤ 7 was compared with the output of the authors’ published code, with no difference; (c) of 49 values of the tables of [5] recomputed, 44 agree to the displayed precision, and 18 of the 22 improved lower bounds attempted are reproduced exactly; the four others (K4(7, 1) by 1, K5(7, 1) by 7, K5(8, 1) and K5(8, 2)) were computed in double precision, and K5(8, 2) ≥ 861 was subsequently reproduced by the multiprecision computation of Section 6.3; (d) no certified bound exceeds the known upper bound of its cell, checked on all 1145 cells of [7]. 6.2. Certificates. A dual feasible point of the program (multipliers yk ≥ 0 for the linear constraints and positive semidefinite matrices Yb for the blocks) proves the bound it attains (Lemma 5). Each numerical dual solution is rounded to rationals with a dyadic denominator, each Yb is displaced into the interior of the semidefinite cone, and if a dual inequality then fails in exact arithmetic the whole dual is multiplied by the largest dyadic θ ≤ 1 that restores feasibility, which multiplies the bound by θ. The certificate is checked by a standalone program (Python standard library only) that rebuilds the program from (q, n, R) in exact integer arithmetic, verifies yk ≥ 0, verifies Yb ⪰ 0 by an exact LDL T factorization over Q, verifies every dual inequality in integer arithmetic, and derives the integer bound by exact comparison of cubes. The checker also verifies the validity of the covering inequality named in the certificate. The checker and the solving pipeline share the transcription of the program of [5] into coefficient generators; an error in that transcription would not be detected by a certificate, which is why the transcription is checked separately by the four tests above. No floating-point computation enters the checker.

Title: [2111.00774] On the number of 𝑞-ary quasi-perfect codes with covering radius 2
URL: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.00774
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
In this paper we present a family of $q$ -ary nonlinear quasi-perfect codes with covering radius 2. The codes have length $n=q^{m}$ and size $M=q^{n-m-1}$ where $q$ is a prime power, $q\geq 3$ , $m$ is an integer, $m\geq 2$ . In this paper we use the switching construction to construct a family of $q$ -ary nonlinear quasi-perfect codes with covering radius $\rho=2$ . The codes we offer are of length $n=q^{m}$ and size $M=q^{n-m-1}$ where $q$ is a prime power, $q\geq 3$ , $m$ is an integer, $m\geq 2$ . In this paper we prove that there are more than $q^{q^{cn}}$ nonequivalent such codes of length $n$ , for all sufficiently large $n$ and a constant $c=\frac{1}{q}-\varepsilon$ .

In [12], using the concatenation construction, a family of $q$ -ary even quasi-perfect codes with covering radius $\rho=2$ was constructed. The codes proposed in [12] have length $n=q^{m}$ and size $M=q^{n-m-1}$ where $q$ is a prime power, $q\geq 3$ , $m$ is an integer, $m\geq 4$ . It was shown [12] that there are more than $q^{q^{cn}}$ nonequivalent such codes of length $n$ , for all sufficiently large $n$ and a constant $c$ .

Proof. The number of words of length $q^{[m]_{q}-m}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ is $q^{q^{[m]_{q}-m}}$ . Hence, by Theorem 7, the number of different quasi-perfect codes with parameters $(n,q^{n-m-1},3;2)_{q}$ is $q^{q^{[m]_{q}-m}}$ . The number of monomial matrices of size $n\times n$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ is $(q-1)^{n}n!$ . Any equivalence class contains not more than $(q-1)^{n}n!\cdot q^{n}$ different quasi-perfect codes with parameters $(n,q^{n-m-1},3;2)_{q}$ . Therefore, there are more than $q^{q^{[m]_{q}-m}-\,n(m+2)}$ nonequivalent $q$ -ary quasi-perfect codes with parameters $(n,q^{n-m-1},3;2)_{q}$ .
